claim: Memory dysfunction is a key symptom of age-related dementia.
source: Memory dysfunction is a key symptom of age-related dementia.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the abstract without specific experimental data from this study.

claim: Acute ventromedial prefrontal cortex stimulation enhanced short-term memory but not long-term memory in the novel-object recognition task.
source: Our results show that acute stimulation enhanced the short-, but not the long-term memory in the novel-object recognition task.
evidence: This claim is directly supported by experimental data presented in the study.

claim: After chronic high-frequency stimulation, both short- and long-term memories were robustly improved in the novel-object recognition test and Morris water-maze spatial task compared to sham.
source: Interestingly, after chronic high-frequency stimulation, both the short- and long-term memories were robustly improved in the novel-object recognition test and Morris water-maze spatial task compared to sham.
evidence: This claim is directly supported by experimental data from behavioral tests.

claim: Chronic ventromedial prefrontal cortex high-frequency stimulation upregulated neurogenesis-associated genes.
source: Our results also demonstrated that chronic ventromedial prefrontal cortex high-frequency stimulation upregulated neurogenesis-associated genes along with enhanced hippocampal cell proliferation.
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data showing gene expression changes.

claim: Chronic ventromedial prefrontal cortex high-frequency stimulation enhanced hippocampal cell proliferation.
source: Our results also demonstrated that chronic ventromedial prefrontal cortex high-frequency stimulation upregulated neurogenesis-associated genes along with enhanced hippocampal cell proliferation.
evidence: This is supported by BrdU and Dcx immunohistochemistry data.

claim: Memory behaviors were strongly correlated with hippocampal neurogenesis.
source: Importantly, these memory behaviors were strongly correlated with the hippocampal neurogenesis.
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis between behavioral measures and neurogenesis markers.

claim: Chronic ventromedial prefrontal cortex high-frequency stimulation may serve as a novel effective therapeutic target for dementia-related disorders.
source: Overall, these findings suggest that chronic ventromedial prefrontal cortex high-frequency stimulation may serve as a novel effective therapeutic target for dementia-related disorders.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the experimental findings.

claim: The prevalence of dementia doubles from a low rate in 60–64 age group to 40–50% of those older than 85.
source: Its prevalence doubles from a low rate in 60–64 age group to 40–50% of those older than 85 (Lobo et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Pharmacological treatments for dementia have limited effects.
source: To date, pharmacological treatments for dementia have limited effects and there are no known treatments that cure or delay the progression of this memory impairment (Doody et al., 2014; Salloway et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: There are no known treatments that cure or delay the progression of memory impairment in dementia.
source: To date, pharmacological treatments for dementia have limited effects and there are no known treatments that cure or delay the progression of this memory impairment (Doody et al., 2014; Salloway et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Deep brain stimulation is currently considered as an alternative treatment to reduce the symptomatic and progression of memory deterioration.
source: Therefore, a novel non-pharmacological approach such as deep brain stimulation (DBS) is currently considered as an alternative treatment to reduce the symptomatic and progression of this memory deterioration (Hescham et al., 2013a).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: DBS has been demonstrated to control a wide range of neurological disorders and neuropsychiatric diseases.
source: DBS, a technique of minimally invasive surgical implantation of electrodes with delivering of electrical impulses into the brain, has been demonstrated to control a wide range of neurological disorders and neuropsychiatric diseases (Sesia et al., 2009; Temel et al., 2012b; Temel and Lim, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: DBS might enhance memory functions when particular brain areas are stimulated.
source: In line with these developments, evidence from recent studies suggests that DBS might enhance memory functions when particular brain areas are stimulated (Hamani et al., 2008; Laxton et al., 2010; Suthana et al., 2012; Hescham et al., 2013b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: DBS of the subgenual anterior cingulate cortex or the ventromedial prefrontal cortex induced striking antidepressant activity in both patients and animal studies.
source: Of particular interest, DBS of the subgenual anterior cingulate cortex or the ventromedial prefrontal cortex (vmPFC) induced striking antidepressant activity in both patients and animal studies (Mayberg et al., 2005; Lozano et al., 2008; Hamani et al., 2010b; Kennedy et al., 2011; Temel and Lim, 2013; Lim et al., 2015b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: No studies have shown the putative role of vmPFC DBS in learning and memory performance.
source: Despite encouraging results, no studies have shown the putative role of vmPFC DBS in learning and memory performance.
evidence: This is a statement about the absence of prior research, based on literature review.

claim: vmPFC plays an important role in the formation, consolidation, and retrieval of memory, as well as reward and decision making.
source: In the realm of cognitive function, there is empirical evidence indicating that vmPFC plays an important role in the formation, consolidation, and retrieval of memory, as well as reward and decision making (Maviel et al., 2004; Euston et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The vmPFC was significantly activated during the recall of remote memory.
source: Based on the human imaging and rodent studies, the vmPFC was significantly activated during the recall of remote memory (Bontempi et al., 1999; Takashima et al., 2006a, 2006b; Gais et al., 2007)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous imaging and rodent studies.

claim: Inactivation of vmPFC caused memory impairment when tested in the radial arm-maze.
source: while its inactivation caused memory impairment when tested in the radial arm-maze (Maviel et al., 2004), the Morris water-maze (MWM) (Teixeira et al., 2006), and the contextual fear conditioning (Frankland et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Inactivation of vmPFC caused memory impairment when tested in the Morris water-maze.
source: while its inactivation caused memory impairment when tested in the radial arm-maze (Maviel et al., 2004), the Morris water-maze (MWM) (Teixeira et al., 2006), and the contextual fear conditioning (Frankland et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Inactivation of vmPFC caused memory impairment when tested in contextual fear conditioning.
source: while its inactivation caused memory impairment when tested in the radial arm-maze (Maviel et al., 2004), the Morris water-maze (MWM) (Teixeira et al., 2006), and the contextual fear conditioning (Frankland et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Malfunctioning has been reported in the hippocampus and the vmPFC in early stages of Alzheimer's disease, frontotemporal dementia, and healthy aging-related memory impairments.
source: In line with these studies, malfunctioning has also been reported in the hippocampus and the vmPFC (which received robust projections from the hippocampal formation) in early stages of Alzheimer's disease, frontotemporal dementia, and healthy aging-related memory impairments (Salat et al., 2001; Lindberg et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: DBS increases hippocampal brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF) levels.
source: Given the potential mechanisms involved by DBS including the increase of hippocampal brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF) levels (Hamani et al., 2012; Ying et al., 2012)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: DBS is involved in neurogenesis-related functions.
source: and neurogenesis-related functions (Toda et al., 2008; Kadar et al., 2011; Stone et al., 2011)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Aged-related deficits occur in both memory and hippocampal functioning.
source: The use of this animal model was supported by previous data that showed aged-related deficits in both the memory and the hippocampal functioning (Rex et al., 2005; Kaczorowski and Disterhoft, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Middle-aged rats show memory deficits compared to young rats.
source: Progressive age-related memory decline has been previously described for human (Davis et al., 2003) and animal studies (Sloane et al., 1997; Ward et al., 1999; Kaczorowski and Disterhoft, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations and experimental data from the NOR test comparing young and middle-aged rats.

claim: Young animals spent relatively more time with the novel object as compared to the familiar object in both the short- and long-term phase.
source: Interestingly, the young animals spent relatively more time with the novel object as compared to the familiar object in both the short- (t(18) = −5.23, p < 0.001) and long-term (t(14) = −8.722, p < 0.001) phase (Figure 1C,D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from the NOR test and shown in Figure 1C,D.

claim: In the middle-aged rats, no significant effect was found for discrimination between the novel and familiar objects in the short- and long-term memory retention interval.
source: In the middle-aged rats, no significant effect was found for discrimination between the novel and familiar objects in the short- and long-term memory retention interval (all t(11) > −2.058, p = n.s.), indicating a possible manifestation of memory deficit in the middle-aged animals.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from the NOR test.

claim: There was a decrease of time spent in the novel object exploration in the middle-aged animals as compared to the young rats.
source: Note: there was a decrease of time spent in the novel object exploration in the middle-aged animals as compared to the young rats, suggesting a possible manifestation of memory deficit in this animal model.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1 and described in the text.

claim: HFS at 200 μA significantly increased the duration of novel object exploration in the short-term memory when compared to the sham.
source: In acute HFS, stimulation at 200 μA significantly increased the duration of novel object exploration in the short- (F(4,39) = 7.995, p < 0.001), but not the long-term (F(4,39) = 1.553, p = n.s.) memory when compared to the sham (Figure 2A,B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from the NOR test and shown in Figure 2A,B.

claim: LFS at 50, 200, and 400 μA induced a longer duration of novel object exploration in the short-term memory when compared to the sham.
source: In acute LFS, stimulation at 50, 200, and 400 μA induced a longer duration of novel object exploration in the short-term memory (F(4,49) = 4,432, p = 0.004) when compared to the sham (Figure 2C,D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from the NOR test and shown in Figure 2C,D.

claim: Animals that tested with no-HFS prior to the behavioral testing spent significantly longer duration exploring novel object in the short-term retention interval when compared to the sham group.
source: After chronic stimulation, animals that tested with no-HFS prior to the behavioral testing, spent significantly longer duration exploring novel object in the short- (t(16) = 2.981, p = 0.009), but not the long-term (t(15) = 1.656, p = n.s.) retention intervals (Figure 3A,B) when compared to the sham group.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from the NOR test and shown in Figure 3A,B.

claim: Animals that were treated with HFS prior to the behavioral testing showed remarkable increase in the novel object exploration for both the short- and long-term intervals as compared to the sham.
source: Interestingly, animals that were treated with HFS prior to the behavioral testing, showed remarkable increase in the novel object exploration for both the short- (t(15) = 2.686, p = 0.017) and long-term (t(14) = 3.783, p = 0.002) intervals as compared to the sham (Figure 3C,D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from the NOR test and shown in Figure 3C,D.

claim: Animals treated with vmPFC HFS exhibited a shorter latency to reach the hidden platform on day 1 and day 2 as compared to the sham group.
source: When analyzing the training phase from days 1 to 4, animals treated with vmPFC HFS exhibited a shorter latency to reach the hidden platform on day 1 (t(17) = −2.348, p = 0.031) and day 2 (t(17) = −2.810, p = 0.012) as compared to the sham group (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from the MWM test and shown in Figure 3E.

claim: vmPFC HFS rats spent more time in the target quadrant during the probe test.
source: In the probe test, vmPFC HFS rats spent more time in the target quadrant (t(17) = 2.511, p = 0.022) and lesser time in the opposite quadrant (t(17) = −2.713, p = 0.015), suggesting that treated rats had stronger spatial memory for the target quadrant (Figure 3F,G).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from the MWM probe test and shown in Figure 3F,G.

claim: vmPFC HFS upregulated genes related with neurogenesis and neuroplasticity (NeuN/Rbfox3, Syn, Dcx, Nes).
source: Remarkably, vmPFC HFS upregulated genes related with neurogenesis and neuroplasticity (NeuN/Rbfox3, t(10) = −7.018, p < 0.001; Syn, t(10) = −4.660, p = 0.001; Dcx, t(10) = −2.860, p = 0.012; Nes, t(10) = −3.214, p = 0.009)
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data.

claim: vmPFC HFS upregulated genes related with neuronal differentiation (Angpt2, S100a4).
source: genes related with neuronal differentiation (Angpt2, t(10) = −3.520, p = 0.006; and S100a4, t(10) = −3.372, p = 0.007)
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data.

claim: vmPFC HFS upregulated genes related with migration and neuroprotective functions (Angpt2).
source: as well as genes related with migration and neuroprotective functions (Angpt2: t(10) = −3.520, p = 0.006) in the hippocampus (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data and shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The gene expression for Syn was significantly correlated with the Nes and Dcx genes.
source: Interestingly, the gene expression for Syn was significantly correlated with the Nes and Dcx genes (all r2 > −0.831, p < 0.046; Figure 4C,D), indicating a close association between these genes for induction of neuroplasticity in the hippocampus after chronic vmPFC HFS.
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis and shown in Figure 4C,D.

claim: vmPFC HFS increased the number of c-Fos-ir positive cells in the subiculum.
source: Our results revealed that vmPFC HFS increased the number of c-Fos-ir positive cells in the subiculum (t(10) = 2.239, p = 0.049), DG (t(10) = 2.992, p = 0.015), along with a marginal difference in the CA1 field (t(10) = 2.131, p = 0.059) of the hippocampus as compared to the non-stimulated sham (Figure 5A,B).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data and shown in Figure 5A,B.

claim: vmPFC HFS increased the number of c-Fos-ir positive cells in the DG.
source: Our results revealed that vmPFC HFS increased the number of c-Fos-ir positive cells in the subiculum (t(10) = 2.239, p = 0.049), DG (t(10) = 2.992, p = 0.015), along with a marginal difference in the CA1 field (t(10) = 2.131, p = 0.059) of the hippocampus as compared to the non-stimulated sham (Figure 5A,B).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data and shown in Figure 5A,B.

claim: The c-Fos-ir in the DG was positively correlated with both the hippocampal SUB and CA1 field.
source: During correlational analysis of the hippocampal neuronal activity, the c-Fos-ir in the DG was positively correlated with both the hippocampal SUB and CA1 field (all r2 > 0.810, p < 0.015), indicating a strong relationship of the DG with the SUB and CA1 regions after vmPFC HFS (Figure 5C,D).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis and shown in Figure 5C,D.

claim: There was a significant increase of surviving BrdU-positive cells after chronic vmPFC HFS as compared to the sham.
source: Our results showed a significant increase of surviving BrdU-positive cells after chronic vmPFC HFS as compared to the sham (t(14) = 4.371, p = 0.001; Figure 5E,F).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data and shown in Figure 5E,F.

claim: There was a remarkable increase in the proliferation of the neural progenitor cells following chronic vmPFC HFS as demonstrated by Dcx.
source: Moreover, there was also a remarkable increase in the proliferation of the neural progenitor cells following chronic vmPFC HFS as demonstrated by an early postmitotic neuronal marker Dcx (t(10) = 4.312, p = 0.002; Figure 5G,H).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data and shown in Figure 5G,H.

claim: There was a significant positive correlation between the BrdU and Dcx cell count in the vmPFC HFS.
source: Interestingly, we found a significant positive correlation between the BrdU and Dcx cell count in the vmPFC HFS (r2 = 0.728, p = 0.031) (Figure 5I).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis and shown in Figure 5I.

claim: After chronic vmPFC HFS, there was an increase of dendritic spine density in the secondary branch of the Golgi-impregnated cells in the DG area of the hippocampus as compared to the sham.
source: Further, after chronic vmPFC HFS, our data demonstrated an increase of dendritic spine density in the secondary (Z = −2.121, p = 0.034), but not the primary branch (Z = −1.061, p = n.s.) of the Golgi-impregnated cells in the DG area of the hippocampus as compared to the sham (Figure 6A,B).
evidence: This is supported by Golgi staining data and shown in Figure 6A,B.

claim: Qualitative evaluation of the immunofluorescence double-labeling showed co-localization of c-Fos with the Dcx and the BrdU labeled cells in the hippocampal DG region of the vmPFC HFS animals.
source: To further investigate the effects of DBS-induced neurogenesis increase for memory function, qualitative evaluation of the immunofluorescence double-labeling showed co-localization of c-Fos with the Dcx and the BrdU labeled cells in the hippocampal DG region of the vmPFC HFS animals (Figure 6C)
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data and shown in Figure 6C.

claim: vmPFC HFS induced a significant positive correlation between the MWM target quadrant and the Dcx cell count.
source: To examine the relationship between the neuroplasticity variables and the memory performances, vmPFC HFS induced a significant positive correlation between the MWM target quadrant and the Dcx cell count (r2 = 0.672, p = 0.046; Figure 7A).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis and shown in Figure 7A.

claim: After chronic vmPFC HFS, there was a positive correlation for the short-term memory in condition of no-HFS prior to the NOR testing with the Dcx cell count.
source: Interestingly, after chronic vmPFC HFS, there was also a positive correlation for the short-term memory in condition of no-HFS prior to the NOR testing with the Dcx cell count (r2 = 0.674, p = 0.045) and NeuN/Rbfox3 gene expression (r2 = 0.834, p = 0.011) (Figure 7C,D).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis and shown in Figure 7C,D.

claim: After chronic vmPFC HFS, there was a positive correlation for the short-term memory in condition of no-HFS prior to the NOR testing with NeuN/Rbfox3 gene expression.
source: Interestingly, after chronic vmPFC HFS, there was also a positive correlation for the short-term memory in condition of no-HFS prior to the NOR testing with the Dcx cell count (r2 = 0.674, p = 0.045) and NeuN/Rbfox3 gene expression (r2 = 0.834, p = 0.011) (Figure 7C,D).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis and shown in Figure 7C,D.

claim: The behavioral effects of vmPFC stimulation were dependent on the stimulation frequency and current intensity.
source: In the acute stimulation experiment, we found that the behavioral effects of vmPFC stimulation were dependent on the stimulation frequency and current intensity.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing different effects at different stimulation parameters.

claim: The mechanisms of the stimulation parameter dependency in regulation of memory functions remain largely obscure.
source: Although these findings are consistent with previous reports (Hamani et al., 2010a; Hescham et al., 2013b), the mechanisms of the stimulation parameter dependency in regulation of memory functions remain largely obscure.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge.

claim: The neurons in the vmPFC are highly sensitive to specific stimulation settings for induction of either long-term potentiation (LTP) or depression (LTD).
source: Nonetheless, it is postulated that the neurons in the vmPFC are highly sensitive to specific stimulation settings for induction of either long-term potentiation (LTP) or depression (LTD).
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on inference from the data.

claim: The vmPFC synapses are potentially vulnerable to LTP or LTD strengthening after specific type of stimulation.
source: This notion was highly supported by the findings in which the vmPFC synapses are potentially vulnerable to LTP or LTD strengthening after specific type of stimulation (Herry and Garcia, 2002).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: The prefrontal cortex neurons could undergo LTP with rapid and stable potentiation in the prelimbic synapses after high-frequency tetanic stimulation of the hippocampal CA1/subicular region.
source: It has been found that the prefrontal cortex neurons could undergo LTP with rapid and stable potentiation in the prelimbic synapses after high-frequency tetanic stimulation of the hippocampal CA1/subicular region (Laroche et al., 1990).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: LTP-like plasticity in the vmPFC after hippocampal HFS has been shown to be dependent on AMPA and NMDA-receptor.
source: Such a LTP-like plasticity in the vmPFC after hippocampal HFS has been shown to be dependent on α-amino-3-hydroxy-5-methyl-4-isoxazole propionic acid (AMPA) and N-methyl-D-aspartate (NMDA)-receptor, which indicates a crucial role for the synaptic potentiation in the hippocampal-vmPFC pathway in rapid memory consolidation (Laroche et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: LFS induced negative effects on the anxiety-related behaviors.
source: Although HFS and LFS at specific amplitudes were effective for memory enhancement, it is noteworthy that LFS induced negative effects on the anxiety-related behaviors (Lim et al., 2015b).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: HFS of the vmPFC has been shown to reduce conditioned fear and enhance the extinction of aversive memory.
source: Furthermore, HFS of the vmPFC has been shown to reduce conditioned fear and enhance the extinction of aversive memory (Milad and Quirk, 2002; Milad et al., 2004)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: LFS induced impairment in extinction of conditioned fear.
source: in contrast to LFS, which induced impairment in extinction of conditioned fear (Shehadi and Maroun, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Previous studies of vmPFC HFS produced robust antidepressant-like behaviors.
source: Since previous studies of vmPFC HFS produced robust antidepressant-like behaviors (Lim et al., 2015a, 2015b)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: vmPFC is involved in the expression of long-term memory.
source: Albeit many studies have indicated that vmPFC is involved in the expression of long-term memory (Maviel et al., 2004; Teixeira et al., 2006)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: vmPFC is involved in consolidation and retrieval of recently acquired memories.
source: there are also findings supporting that vmPFC is involved in consolidation and retrieval of recently acquired memories (Blum et al., 2006; Leon et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The vmPFC HFS potentiated the initial hippocampal encoding during the acquisition phase, which was then followed by enhanced retrieval during the short- and long-term memory recalls.
source: Thus, it is likely that the vmPFC HFS potentiated the initial hippocampal encoding during the acquisition phase, which was then followed by enhanced retrieval during the short- and long-term memory recalls.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental results.

claim: HFS of the vmPFC induced profound antidepressant-like behaviors in the experimental animal studies.
source: HFS of the vmPFC has not only been demonstrated for memory enhancement in the middle-aged memory deficit rat model, but also induced profound antidepressant-like behaviors in the experimental animal studies (Lim et al., 2015a; 2015b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The effects of memory improvement by vmPFC HFS were highly associated with the stimulation effects on reduction in anxiety behavior.
source: Interestingly, the effects of memory improvement by vmPFC HFS, as characterized by the increased novelty seeking in the NOR and MWM tasks, were highly associated with the stimulation effects on reduction in anxiety behavior.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental results and previous findings.

claim: Animals with lower anxiety or fear level displayed higher novelty seeking behavior.
source: These results confirm previous findings that animals with lower anxiety or fear level displayed higher novelty seeking behavior, particularly in the elevated plus-maze and light–dark box tests (Kabbaj et al., 2000; Stead et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Rats undergoing chronic stress exhibited anxious and low exploratory behaviors.
source: In consistent with the data found in the animal model of depression, rats undergoing chronic stress exhibited anxious and low exploratory behaviors (Lim et al., 2015b), as well as impairment in spatial memory task performances (Conrad et al., 1996; Beck and Luine, 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Chronic stress produces pathological alterations on the molecular and morphological levels in the hippocampus that is involved in the regulation of both the spatial memory formation and emotional behaviors.
source: Apparently, chronic stress produces pathological alterations on the molecular and morphological levels in the hippocampus that is involved in the regulation of both the spatial memory formation and emotional behaviors.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge and previous studies.

claim: The memory enhancement effect is likely to be accompanied by the vmPFC DBS-induced anxiolytic effects via the mechanisms of neurogenesis and dendritic remodeling in the hippocampal neurons.
source: Thus, our experiments found that the memory enhancement effect is likely to be accompanied by the vmPFC DBS-induced anxiolytic effects via the mechanisms of neurogenesis and dendritic remodeling in the hippocampal neurons.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental results.

claim: vmPFC HFS drove the local neural activity as characterized by c-Fos-ir activation in the subiculum, DG, as well as a marginal increase in the CA1 field of the hippocampus.
source: Given the prominent anatomical connectivity between the hippocampus and vmPFC (Jay and Witter, 1991; Cenquizca and Swanson, 2007), it was observed that vmPFC HFS drove the local neural activity as characterized by c-Fos-ir activation in the subiculum, DG, as well as a marginal increase in the CA1 field of the hippocampus.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and citations to previous anatomical studies.

claim: The effects of vmPFC HFS on the hippocampal neural activity are mediated by a reciprocal bisynaptic pathway through the nucleus reunions or the lateral entorhinal cortex.
source: Although there is no direct connection from vmPFC to the hippocampus, it is possible that the effects of vmPFC HFS on the hippocampal neural activity are mediated by a reciprocal bisynaptic pathway through the nucleus reunions or the lateral entorhinal cortex (Burwell and Amaral, 1998; Vertes et al., 2007).
evidence: This is a speculative inference supported by citations to previous anatomical studies.

claim: The neural activity in the hippocampus could probably be activated by either antidromic or orthodromic stimulation that possibly achieved by a current spread from the vmPFC structure to the neighboring axon bundles—the minor forceps of the corpus callosum.
source: Besides, the neural activity in the hippocampus could probably be activated by either antidromic or orthodromic stimulation that possibly achieved by a current spread from the vmPFC structure to the neighboring axon bundles—the minor forceps of the corpus callosum (Lim et al., 2015b).
evidence: This is a speculative inference supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: HFS of the subgenual cingulate gyrus showed connections to the medial frontal cortex, anterior and posterior cingulate, and the anterior medial temporal lobe (i.e., amygdala-hippocampus).
source: Of particular interest, a tractography analysis by diffusion tensor imaging provides evidence for this structural connectivity that HFS of the subgenual cingulate gyrus (generally considered to be homologue of the rat vmPFC), showed connections to the medial frontal cortex, anterior and posterior cingulate, and the anterior medial temporal lobe (i.e., amygdala-hippocampus) (Gutman et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous imaging study.

claim: The excitatory and inhibitory inputs from the amygdala and hippocampus were converged and interact in the vmPFC.
source: It has been shown that the excitatory and inhibitory inputs from the amygdala and hippocampus were converged and interact in the vmPFC (Ishikawa and Nakamura, 2003)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: The vmPFC and hippocampus theta oscillations were highly synchronized during memory acquisition and retrieval in spatial tasks.
source: More importantly, the electrophysiological studies have provided concrete evidence of functional interaction between the vmPFC and hippocampus in which their theta oscillations were highly synchronized as measured by both the spike-theta phase locking and local field potential coherence, during memory acquisition and retrieval in spatial tasks (Jones and Wilson, 2005; Siapas et al., 2005; Benchenane et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous electrophysiological studies.

claim: The rapid encoding and retrieval of memory depend largely on the bidirectional regulation of synaptic connectivity between the vmPFC and hippocampus.
source: Based on this evidence, we suggested that the rapid encoding and retrieval of memory depend largely on the bidirectional regulation of synaptic connectivity between the vmPFC and hippocampus
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental results and previous studies.

claim: The disruption of connection between vmPFC and hippocampus affects the learning and memory functions, which are commonly identified in patients suffering from dementia.
source: while the disruption of its connection affect the learning and memory functions, which are commonly identified in patients suffering from dementia (Salat et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: HFS of the anterior nucleus of the thalamus and the entorhinal cortex has been demonstrated to increase neurogenesis.
source: In line with our findings, HFS of the anterior nucleus of the thalamus and the entorhinal cortex has been demonstrated to increase neurogenesis (Toda et al., 2008)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: HFS of the anterior nucleus of the thalamus and the entorhinal cortex enhanced memory functions, particularly spatial memory measured in the MWM.
source: and memory functions, particularly spatial memory measured in the MWM (Stone et al., 2011) and enhanced performance on a delayed non-matching to sample task (Hamani et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Chronic HFS has been shown to modulate the hippocampal genes that involved in the proliferation and neurogenesis-related functions, as well as genes supporting for neural differentiation, migration and maturation.
source: In agreement with our previous microarray data (Kadar et al., 2011), chronic HFS has been shown to modulate the hippocampal genes that involved in the proliferation and neurogenesis-related functions, as well as genes supporting for neural differentiation, migration and maturation.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous microarray data and the current qPCR results.

claim: vmPFC HFS induced significant increase of BDNF and serotonin (5-HT) levels in the hippocampus.
source: Further, our present observations were also supported by earlier works demonstrating that vmPFC HFS induced significant increase of BDNF and serotonin (5-HT) levels in the hippocampus (Hamani et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: The increase of 5-HT and BDNF expression in the hippocampus regulate synaptic plasticity, as well as cognitive and mood-related behaviors.
source: Recent studies have shown that the increase of 5-HT and BDNF expression in the hippocampus regulate synaptic plasticity, as well as cognitive and mood-related behaviors.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge from recent studies.

claim: Both the 5-HT and BDNF promote neurogenesis by enhancing the synaptogenesis, neuronal differentiation, and survival particularly for memory acquisition and consolidation.
source: It is well-known that both the 5-HT and BDNF promote neurogenesis by enhancing the synaptogenesis, neuronal differentiation, and survival particularly for memory acquisition and consolidation (Gaspar et al., 2003; Lu and Chang, 2004; Pang et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The increased neurogenesis effects indicate that its plausible mechanism is facilitated by the release of 5-HT and enhanced BDNF levels.
source: Although no microdialysis data were provided with regard to the extracellular levels of 5-HT and BDNF after chronic vmPFC HFS, the increased neurogenesis effects as obtained from this study clearly indicate that its plausible mechanism is facilitated by the release of 5-HT and enhanced BDNF levels (Hamani et al., 2012).
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental results and previous studies.

claim: The increased neurogenesis was highly associated with enhanced learning and memory.
source: In support of this notion, previous studies have demonstrated that the increased neurogenesis was highly associated with enhanced learning and memory, while its decrease caused memory impairment (van Praag et al., 1999; Shors et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: There is a possibility that the DBS-induced memory enhancement effects are mediated by other non-neurogenic mechanisms such as modulation of the neurotransmission, synaptic potentiation by the AMPA/NMDA receptor trafficking, and enhancement of the BDNF or CREB function.
source: Although the present study has identified the DBS-induced memory enhancement by neurogenesis, there is a possibility that these effects are mediated by other non-neurogenic mechanisms such as modulation of the neurotransmission (via acetylcholine, dopamine, 5-HT, etc), synaptic potentiation by the AMPA/NMDA receptor trafficking, and enhancement of the BDNF or CREB (cAMP response element-binding protein) function (Hamani et al., 2012; Stern and Alberni, 2012).
evidence: This is a speculative statement supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: vmPFC HFS might possibly cause an alteration of increased dendritic synaptogenesis, particularly in the hippocampal DG where transcriptional process for Nes and Dcx genes occurs.
source: Our correlation analysis of gene expression revealed that the Syn was strongly associated with the Nes and Dcx genes, suggesting that vmPFC HFS might possibly cause an alteration of increased dendritic synaptogenesis, particularly in the hippocampal DG where transcriptional process for Nes and Dcx genes occurs.
evidence: This is an inference based on correlation analysis of gene expression data.

claim: Electrical stimulation affected the axonal path in cultured Xenopus neurons that was mediated by elevation of both cytoplasmic Ca2+ and cyclic adenosine monophosphate levels.
source: This observation was supported by a previous study which showed that electrical stimulation affected the axonal path in cultured Xenopus neurons that was mediated by elevation of both cytoplasmic Ca2+ and cyclic adenosine monophosphate levels (Ming et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: The spatial memory performances were associated with the cell proliferation in the DG.
source: Importantly, our behavioral correlates show that the spatial memory performances were associated with the cell proliferation in the DG, indicating that neurogenesis in the DG is vital for the hippocampal-dependent learning and memory processes.
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis between behavioral measures and cell proliferation data.

claim: Neurogenesis in the DG is vital for the hippocampal-dependent learning and memory processes.
source: Importantly, our behavioral correlates show that the spatial memory performances were associated with the cell proliferation in the DG, indicating that neurogenesis in the DG is vital for the hippocampal-dependent learning and memory processes.
evidence: This is an inference based on the correlation between neurogenesis and memory performance.

claim: Chronic vmPFC HFS induces long-lasting effects on memory performances and its underlying mechanism is possibly mediated by an enhanced neurogenesis in the hippocampus.
source: In conclusion, our findings suggest that chronic vmPFC HFS induces long-lasting effects on memory performances and its underlying mechanism is possibly mediated by an enhanced neurogenesis in the hippocampus.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental findings.

claim: vmPFC might serve as a new effective DBS target for aged-related memory deficits.
source: Despite the fact that this structure has been previously shown for antidepressant-like activities, it might as well serve as a new effective DBS target for aged-related memory deficits.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the experimental findings.

claim: All electrode tips were verified within the vmPFC target.
source: All localization of electrode tips were verified within the vmPFC target as illustrated in a representative Figure 1B.
evidence: This is supported by histological verification shown in Figure 1B.

claim: There was no difference in the duration of object exploration between young and middle-aged rats in the acquisition phase.
source: With regard to the duration of object exploration, there was no significant difference between the young and middle-aged rats in the acquisition phase (t(28) = −0.742, p = n.s.), see Supplementary file 1A.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from the NOR test.

claim: A decrease in the duration of novel object exploration was observed for the middle-aged group when compared to the young in the long-term memory.
source: However, a decrease in the duration of novel object exploration was observed for the middle-aged group when compared to the young in the long-term (t(26) = 4.129, p < 0.001), but not the short-term (t(29) = 0.014, p = n.s.) memory.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from the NOR test.

claim: No differences were found in the duration of object exploration for both the HFS and the LFS groups in the acquisition phase.
source: In the acquisition phase, no differences were found in the duration of object exploration for both the HFS (F(4,40) = 1.509, p = n.s.) and the LFS (F(4,50) = 0.478, p = n.s.) groups, see Supplementary file 1B,C.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from the NOR test.

claim: The novel object exploration was higher compared to the familiar object after HFS at 200 μA.
source: The novel object exploration was also higher compared to the familiar object (t(9) = −14.636, p < 0.001).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from the NOR test.

claim: LFS at 50, 100, 200, and 400 μA increased the duration of novel object exploration in the short-term memory.
source: Interestingly, for comparisons of discrimination between novel and familiar objects, LFS at 50, 100, 200, and 400 μA (all t(6–11) > −6.250, p < 0.001) increased the duration of novel object exploration in the short-term memory.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from the NOR test.

claim: An increase for novel object exploration was found with LFS at 50, 100, and 200 μA in the long-term memory.
source: In terms of the long-term memory, an increase for novel object exploration was found with LFS at 50, 100, and 200 μA (all t(9–11) > −3.440, p < 0.029), but not at 400 μA (all t(6) = 0.969, p = n.s.) when compared to the familiar object.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from the NOR test.

claim: No differences were found in the exploratory duration for animals that tested in conditions with either no-HFS or HFS prior to the NOR task in the acquisition phase.
source: In the acquisition phase, we found no differences in the exploratory duration for animals that tested in conditions with either no-HFS (t(15) = 1.531, p = n.s.) or HFS (t(14) = 1.272, p = n.s.) prior to the NOR task, see Supplementary file 1D,E.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from the NOR test.

claim: Chronic stimulation induced a significantly higher exploration time for the novel object in the short-term memory.
source: For comparisons between the novel and familiar objects, chronic stimulation induced a significantly higher exploration time for the novel object in the short- (t(9) = −6.710, p < 0.001), but not the long-term memory (t(8) = −1.891, p = 0.095).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from the NOR test.

claim: The duration for novel object exploration compared to the familiar object was significantly increased in both the short- and long-term memory in animals with vmPFC HFS prior to the NOR testing.
source: The duration for novel object exploration compared to the familiar object was also significantly increased in both the short- and long-term memory (all t(9) < −6.190, p < 0.01) in animals with vmPFC HFS prior to the NOR testing.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from the NOR test.

claim: No significant difference was found in the exploration time for familiar object in both the short- and long-term memory between the vmPFC HFS and sham animals.
source: No significant difference was found in the exploration time for familiar object in both the short- and long-term memory (all t(>14) < 0.865, p = n.s.) between the vmPFC HFS and sham animals.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from the NOR test.

claim: No significant difference was found on day 3 and 4 of MWM training as all rats eventually learned the task.
source: No significant difference was found on day 3 and 4 (all t(17) > −1.648, p = n.s.) as all rats eventually learned the task.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from the MWM test.

claim: vmPFC HFS rats spent lesser time in the opposite quadrant during the probe test.
source: In the probe test, vmPFC HFS rats spent more time in the target quadrant (t(17) = 2.511, p = 0.022) and lesser time in the opposite quadrant (t(17) = −2.713, p = 0.015), suggesting that treated rats had stronger spatial memory for the target quadrant (Figure 3F,G).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from the MWM probe test and shown in Figure 3F,G.

claim: No significant difference was demonstrated in other equivalent quadrants during the MWM probe test.
source: No significant difference was demonstrated in other equivalent quadrants (all t(17) > −0.386, p = n.s.).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from the MWM probe test.

claim: No significant effect was found for latency to reach the imaginary platform during the probe test between the vmPFC HFS and sham animals.
source: When analyzing the latency to reach the imaginary platform during the probe test, no significant effect was found between the vmPFC HFS and sham animals (t(16) = −1.505, p = n.s.; Figure 3H).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from the MWM probe test and shown in Figure 3H.

claim: No changes were found for Timp1, Ccl2, and BDNF gene expression after vmPFC HFS.
source: No changes were found for Timp1, Ccl2, and BDNF (all t(10)> −1.781, p = n.s.).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data.

claim: vmPFC HFS induced approximately 4.8-fold increase of Angpt2 gene expression relative to the sham.
source: Calculation for the fold-change values using 2-Delta (Delta Ct) method indicated that vmPFC HFS induced approximately 4.8-fold (Angpt2), 2-fold (NeuN/Rbfox3), and >1-fold (Syn, Dcx, Nes, S100a4) increase of gene expression relative to the sham (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data and shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Although no differences were observed for Timp1, Ccl2, and BDNF genes, their fold-changes were increased by approximately 1.8-fold for Timp1, 2-fold for Ccl2, and 1.2-fold for BDNF.
source: Although no differences were observed for Timp1, Ccl2, and BDNF genes, their fold-changes were increased by approximately 1.8-fold for Timp1, 2-fold for Ccl2, and 1.2-fold for BDNF, respectively.
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data.

claim: Although no effect was shown in the CA3 field of the hippocampus, there was a trend of increased c-Fos-ir neuronal activity after vmPFC stimulation.
source: Although no effect was shown in the CA3 field of the hippocampus (t(10) = 1.610, p = n.s.), there was a trend of increased c-Fos-ir neuronal activity after vmPFC stimulation.
evidence: This is an observation from the immunohistochemistry data.

claim: No significant correlation between the neuronal activity of c-Fos-ir was found in the hippocampus for sham animals.
source: No significant correlation between the neuronal activity of c-Fos-ir was found in the hippocampus for sham animals (all r2 > 0.025, p = n.s.).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis.

claim: There was a marginal increase of spine density found in the secondary branch of the vmPFC HFS animals.
source: In comparison between the dendritic spines of the primary and secondary branch, there was a marginal increase of spine density found in the secondary branch of the vmPFC HFS (Z = −1.826, p = 0.068), but not in the sham (Z = −1.604, p = n.s.) animals.
evidence: This is supported by Golgi staining data.

claim: Co-localization of c-Fos with Dcx and BrdU labeled cells indicates a possibility of a substantial role of these newborn cells in the memory enhancement function.
source: To further investigate the effects of DBS-induced neurogenesis increase for memory function, qualitative evaluation of the immunofluorescence double-labeling showed co-localization of c-Fos with the Dcx and the BrdU labeled cells in the hippocampal DG region of the vmPFC HFS animals (Figure 6C), indicating a possibility of a substantial role of these newborn cells in the memory enhancement function.
evidence: This is an inference based on immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Memory deficits were partly due to the disruption of the hippocampal neuroplasticity.
source: Previous studies have shown that memory deficits were partly due to the disruption of the hippocampal neuroplasticity (Deupree et al., 1993; Rex et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The increased BDNF level and neurogenesis function in the hippocampus were strongly correlated with the hippocampal-dependent memory tests.
source: Further, this hypothesis was also supported by the fact that the increased BDNF level and neurogenesis function in the hippocampus were strongly correlated with the hippocampal-dependent memory tests (Drapeau et al., 2003; Erickson et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.
